cooling propensities. A diet prescribed by an ayurvedic doctor is a health
plan and a cure in itself. The main focus is not the food item’s nutritional
value or its mineral and vitamin content, but rather how it interacts with the
doshas, what its energetic propensities and tastes are, and wether it
harmonizes with the individual’s constitution. Practicioners of the Ayurveda
often utilize herbs as well as diet, keeping in mind the same principles.
According to the Vedas, our diet affects not only our bodies but our mental
balance and emotions as well. Just as stormy, negativ emotions make
digesting more difficult, accordingly, bad digestion affects our emotions. The
Chandogya Upanishad states: „Food that we eat is transformed in three
different ways. Its gross and heaviest substance becomes the excrement; that
of medium density creates the body and the subtle substance forms the
mind. Water also has three layers: its gross substance forms urine, its middle
part builds blood, its subtle essence becomes the life force.”
This is why the Vedas reject meat – it carries the energy of death and
violance; alcohol and caffeinated beverages disturb our emotions and
thoughts.
Diet According to the Doshas
VATA DECREASING DIET
Vata types may suffer from weight loss and the shrinking of tissue in the
instance of a disturbance in that dosha. For them, it is imperative that they
consume good quality food with the right characteristics for their
constitution. Try to eat often, and eat grounding, nourishing food that is
associated with the earth element. These foods are heavy, warm,
strengthening, and moist. Give preference to the sweet, sour and satly tastes.
Eat small meals at regular, short intervals. Vata types get the most benefit
from cooked, warm meals.
Do not sit down to eat while feeling stressed, anxious, or fearful. Vata
types’ dietary habits tend to be the most unregulated, the most whimsical,
therefore it is very important for them to follow regulation when it comes to
eating. Do not skip meals.
Fuit
Since most fruits are pleasant and harmonizing, they are beneficial for vata

types. Dry fruit are an exception.
Good: grapefruit, banana, orange, papaya, pineapple, mango, figs,
apples (cooked in a light syrup), plums, apricots, cherries, dates,
lemon, lime, peaches, pears, pomegranates, raspberries, strawberries.
Counter-recommended: raw apples, dry fruits, watermelon,
blueberries.
Vegetables
Vata types can eat most vegetables as long as they are cooked, but shouldn’t
eat them on their own, or their bodies become too light. They should dress
their vegetables with oils and spices, and accompany them with grains.
Restrict raw salads, and eat them with a lot of dressing and oil.
Good: avocados, beets, carrots, fresh corn, green beans, okra, parsley,
fresh green peas, summer squash, radishes, sweet potatoes,
horseradish, black olives
Counter-recommended: artichokes, asparagus, bell peppers, broccoli,
brussel sprouts, cauliflower, celeriac, swiss chard, eggplants, chol rabi,
green olives.
Grains
Most grains are nourising and heavy, therefore beneficial for vata types. A
diet of whole grains can prevent a lot of vata related ailments.
Good: basmati rice, brown rice, cous cous, oats, wheat, amaranth,
quinoa.
Counter-recommended: granola and flaked grains, barley,
buckwheat, corn, millet, rye, tapioca.
Legumes
Most legumes cause bloating, thus aggravating vata.
Good: mung beans, tofu.
Counter-recommended: chickpeas, soy, yellow split peas, urad dal,
lime beans, kidney beans.

Nuts and Seeds
Good: almonds, brazil nuts, cashew nuts, peanuts, pecans, pine nuts,
pistachios, sesame seeds, walnuts, sunflower seeds, coconut, pumpkin
seeds.
Counter-recommended: none
Milk Products
Most milk products are heavy, nourishing and moist, thus decreasing vata.
For vata types, fermented milk products are the most beneficial, since they
are pre-digested.
Good: butter, milk curds, paneer (Indian style fresh cheese), ghee,
kefir, milk, sour cream, yogurt, buttercream, cheese, rice milk, goat
milk.
Counter-recommended: ice cream, soy milk, milk powder.
Oils
Most oils help vata types. Their warm and moist qualities are excellent
counterpoints to the cold and dry nature of vata dosha, therefore oils are the
most highly recommended form of food for vata types.
Good: almond oil, avocado oil, butter, ghee, olive oil, sesame oil,
peanut butter, coconut oil, flex oil.
Counter-recommended: margarin, soy oil, corn oil, canola oil.
Sweeteners
Most sweeteners and sweets are well suited for vata types. They need more of
the sweet taste than others in order to build and strengthen tissue.
Good: fructose, raw cane sugar, maple syrup, molasses, raw sugar,
honey.
Counter-recommended: processed white sugar.
Spices
Spices regulate the appetite of vata types, and help alleviate the symptoms of
bloating. They are best added to sweet and heavy food, to help move

digestion along.
Good: asafoetida, basil, bay leaves, cardamom, cloves, coriander,
caraway seeds, cinnamon, fennel, fenugreek seeds, garlic, saffron,
oregano, nutmeg, sage, black peppers, cayenne peppers, dill,
horseradish, mint, mustard, paprika, rosemary, soy sauce, turmeric.
Counter-recommended: none.
Beverages
Vata types should be especially careful to stay hydrated. Besides water, they
should drink milk products, herbal teas, sour fruit juices and lemon or lime
water for hydration as well as nourishment.
Vitamins and Minerals
Vata types need oil soluable vitamins (for example A, D, and E) as well as
vitamin C. Among minerals, zink and calcium are the most important.
PITTA DECREASING DIET
Pitta types, famous for their appetite, need a slightly dry and somewhat rich
diet. The effects of bad diet manifest not as a bad stomach, but rather as
inflammatory diseases. The sweet, bitter and astringent tastes decrease pitta.
The sour, salty and pungent tastes make the fire burn stronger.
People with pitta constitution should avoid strong flavors. It is best to eat
raw, cold food, lightly spiced. Don’t use too much oil for cooking. Avoid
overcooked and deep fried food, do not burden the liver with food that is
difficult to digest.
Before one sits down to eat, one should put aside anger and irritation.
Three meals a day are generally sufficient for pitta types. Do not eat late at
night.
Fruits
Most fruits – due to their calming, cooling effect – are beneficial for pitta
types.
Good: apples, cranberries, dates, figs, grapes, cantalopes, watermelon,
sweet oranges, pears, pineapple, pomegranates, plums, raspberries,

mango.
Counter-recommended: cherries, sour cherries, grapefruit, lemon,
apricots, peaches, banana, strawberries.
Vegetables
Most vegetables are suitable for pitta types even raw. In the winter, though,
it is more prudent to cook them. They may be sauteed in a little bit of ghee,
but don’t deep fry them.
Good: artichokes, asparagus, paprika, broccoli, brussel sprouts,
cauliflower, cabbage, celery, cilantro, fresh sweet corn, cucumbers,
green beans, savoy cabbage, lettuce, okra, parsley, green peas,
summer squash, potatoes, eggplant, zucchini.
Counter-recommended: avocado, beets, carrots, swiss chard,
spinach, chilli peppers, onions, radishes, spinach, sweet potatoes,
tomatoes, horseradish, khol rabi.
Grains
Most whole grains are suitable for pitta types. They are nourishing and
strengthening, but not too warming.
Good: barley, basmati rice, cous cous, millet, wheat, oats, granola,
quinoa, amarant, tapioca.
Counter-recommended: brown rice, buckwheat, sweet corn, rye.
Legumes
Of most people, pitta types digest legumes most easily, but even they benefit
from using some spices in their bean dishes.
Good: chickpeas, mung beans, tofu, kidney beans, lime beans, yellow
split peas.
Counter-recommended: lentils, urad dal.
Nuts and Seeds
Nuts are oily and warming. They increase the fire, therefore, as a rule, they
are not recommeded for pitta types.

Good: coconuts, sunflower seeds.
Counter-recommended: almonds, brazil nuts, cashew nuts, peanuts,
pecans, walnuts, sesame seeds, pumpkin seeds, pine nuts.
Oils
Oil’s nature is pitta, therefore pitta types should use it in moderation.
Good: butter, coconut oil, ghee, sunflower oil, soy oil.
Counter-recommended: almond oil, peanut butter, sesame oil,
mustard oil, canola oil, corn oil, flex oil, olive oil, margarin.
Milk Products
Of all people, it is easiest for pitta types to digest milk products. An
occassional fast that involves drinking milk benefits not only their bodies,
but their minds as well.
Good: milk curds, cream, paneer (Indian style fresh cheese), milk,
ricemilk, soy milk, cheese (fresh cheeses).
Counter-recommended: aged cheese, kefir, sour cream, yogurt,
buttercream, ice cream.
Sweeteners
Good: raw sugar, fructose, maple syrup, raw honey, cane sugar, rice
syrup, date syrup.
Counter-recommended: aged honey, molasses, refined sugar.
Spices
Spicy food greatly increases pitta, therefore pitta types should eat neutral or
cooling spices.
Good: cilantro, coriander, dill, fennel, saffron, caraway seeds,
turmeric, rosemary, mint, cloves.
Counter-recommended: asafoetida, black peppers, cayenne pepper,
garlic, mustard, oregano, chilli peppers, tamarind, soy sauce, sage,
cinnamon, fenugreek seeds, bay leaves, basil, ginger.

Beverages
Pitta types need to drink a lot. The best beverage for them is cool spring
water. Astringent herbal teas are also recommended, such as rasberry leaf,
dandelion, hibiscus, greater celandine, and mint. Milk based beverages are
just as nourishing as certain fruit juices, such as pineapple, pomagranate or
blueberry juice. Alcohol and coffe are harmful.
Vitamins and Minerals
Since pitta types digest raw vegetables easily, they get enough nourishment
from their food and don’t usually need to supplement vitamins. Still, they
may benefit by taking vitamin B, K, and A. Iron and calcium are helpful
mineral supplements for them.
KAPHA DECREASING DIET
A diet that is suitable for kapha types is warm, light and dry. They should
avoid food that is greasy, heavy, or cold. Mucus is a sign that one has eaten
too much kapha aggrevating food. Kapha is increased by the sweet, salty and
and sour tastes, and is decreased by pungent, bitter and astringent tastes.
Kapha types need less food, less frequently. Ideally, they should eat three
times a day; the main meal should be consumed in the middle of the day, the
other two meals should be very light. Don’t eat anything at night, especially
heavy food. Fasting once a week is recommended.
Fruits
Fruit increases the water content of the body, and that can lead to the
accumulation of mucus. For those reasons, they are not especially good for
kapha types.
Good: dried fruit , apples, cranberries, pomegranates.
Counter-recommended: cherries, dates, grapes, bananas, mangos,
watermelons, oranges, pineapples, plums, raspberries, strawberries,
peaches, pears, papayas, lemons, limes, blueberries, grapefruits.
Vegetables
Almost all vegetables are good for kapha types, as long as they are steamed,
warm, and are served with spices.

Good: artichokes, asparagus, beets, paprika, broccoli, brussel sprouts,
cabbage, carrots, cauliflower, celery, swiss chard, eggplant, green
beans, chilli peppers, lettuce, mushrooms, parsley, cilantro, green
peas, potatoes, radishes, spinach, horseradish.
Counter-recommended: avocado, fresh sweet corn, cucumbers, okra,
summer squash, sweet potatoes, tomatoes, winter squash, zucchini,
olives.
Grains
Grains are considered heavy, therefore they are not recommended for kapha
types.
Good: barley, buckwheat, sweet corn, flaked or puffed cereal, millet,
rye, amarant, quinoa, tapioca.
Counter-recommended: basmati rice, brown rice, cous cous, oats,
wheat, white rice, pasta.
Legumes
Most legumes, eaten hot, are suitable for kapha types.
Good: kidney beans, mung beans, soy, yellow split peas, tofu, lima
beans, lentils.
Counter-recommended: chickpeas.
Nuts and Seeds
Most nuts and seeds are heavy and are not beneficial for kapha types.
Good: pumpkin seeds, sunflower seeds.
Counter-recommended: almonds, brazil nuts, cashew nuts, coconuts,
peanuts, pecans, pine nuts, sesame seeds, walnuts.
Oils
Most oils are moist and heavy, and therefore are not recommended for kapha
types. They may consume oils in small quantities.
Good: canola oil, corn oil, flex oil, mustard oil, sunflower oil.
Counter-recommended: almond oil, butter, ghee, margarin, olive oil,

peanut butter, sesame oil.
Milk Products
Milk creates mucus and can be an allergent. It would serve kapha types well
to eliminate milk products from their diet.
Good: soy milk, goat milk, buttermilk.
Counter-recommended: cheese, milk curds, milk, cream, ice cream,
kefir, rice milk, sour cream, yogurt.
Sweeteners
The sweet flavor is the most harmful for kapha type people. This may be the
primary cause of their ailments.
Good: aged honey.
Counter-recommended: fructose, raw honey, cane sugar, molasses,
maple syrup, refined sugar.
Spices
All spices are perfect for kapha types. Warm, hot spices speed up metabolism
and stop liquid from accumulating in the tissue.
Good: asafoetida, basil, bay leaves, black peppers, cardamom, cayenne
peppers, cilantro, cinnamon, cloves, coriander, caraway seeds, dill,
fennel, fenugreek seeds, garlic, ginger, horseradish, mint, mustard,
nutmeg, oregano, paprika, parsley, rosemary, saffron, sage, soy sauce,
turmeric.
Counter-recommended: salt, tamarind.
Beverages
Kapha-types need less water. They should avoid cold water and ice, and
consume warm teas instead. Spiced teas are especially good (ginger tea,
cinnamon tea, dandelion, chicory).
Vitamins and Minerals
Kapha types don’t need a lot of extra vitamins and minerals. Vitamin B-s can
be beneficial.

Lifestyle According to the Three Doshas –
A Summary
VATA
The key word is routine.
They need peace and de-stressing.
A good physical excercise for them is running.
Vata type people should use sweet and calming herbs such as fennel,
licorice, and lemon balm to promote restful sleep.
Vata types should keep their bodies warm at all times, winter and
summer.
They should use sweet, warming spices, such as ginger, cinnamon, and
nutmeg.
Vata types benefit from visits to a sauna, steam teraphy and massage
with sesame oil.
They should eat many small meals during the day, consisting of heavy,
oily food that taste sweet, salty and sour. Consume pungent, bitter and
astringent tastes in moderation.
Fasting is not recommended for vata types.
PITTA
The key word is moderation.
Pitta types need peace, and should minimize stress.
Good forms of physical excercize for them are hatha yoga, martial
arts, tennis.
Pitta types should restrict the consumption of stimulants and drink
calming, inflammation reducing herbal teas instead.
Avoid strong spices and use herbs and mild spices instead.
Pitta types should eat three times a day, giving preferance to food
with bitter, astringent and sweet tastes. Consume pungent, salty and
sour tastes in moderation.
KAPHA

The key word is motivation.
When kapha type people aren’t motivated, they become depressed.
They need a good trainer or a fitness buddy to keep them motivated
for excercize. Excercize is very important for them. It is crucial that
they incorporate at least a daily walk into their lives.
Kapha types should use hot pads and drying herbs like chamomile and
mustard oil. These heat and dry the body.
Too much attachment leads to excessive kapha dosha.
Three daily meals are recommended, but only lunch should be
substantial. Kapha type people should eat cooked, warm and light
food, giving preference to the pungent, bitter and astringent tastes.
Moderate the consumption of sour, salty and sweet tastes.
Ayurvedic Lifestyle from an Ecological
Viewpoint
As I have mentioned before, Ayurveda lists three things that contribute to
the preservation of health. This book is about the Ayurvedic diet (ahara), but
I would like to briefly discuss healthy lifestyle (vihara), too. I will only touch
this wide topic.
Ayurveda stresses that we should live in harmony with nature, follow the
seasons, eat locally grown produce. In the modern world it doesn’t matter
what grows where and when. Grocery stores sell strawberries and
watermelons in January and one can get okras or bitter melon anywhere.
A healthy lifestyle means that we are in tune with the earth and the
seasons. We cook with whatever happens to grow in the garden or is
available at the farmer’s market. Instead of stalking speciality stores for
exotic ingredients, we cook with cauliflowers, carrots and grean beans. Why
is this important?
Bite into a strawberry in January. Even with closed eyes we will be able to
tell the difference between it, and its locally grown counterpart in season. It
doesn’t feel nutritious the same way, does it? During the summer months we
should consume as many vegetables and fruits as possible in order to store
up on vitamins and minerals for the cold weather when produce doesn’t
grow.

Seasonal, local produce is enviromentally friendly, since it doesn’t require
packaging and transportation. It is also budget friendly: a quart of local
strawberries are considerably cheaper than imported ones in January.
This is what this cookbook is about. It encourages you to cook with local,

be able to prepare Indian or Ayurvedic dishes. The same is true of dosha

too involved, enlist the help of a trained Ayurvedic practicioner.
Dear reader! It is my sincere hope that this book will be helpful in
harmonizing your doshas as well as in creating harmony in your everyday
life

Indian Cuisine
The sensory experiences associated with Indian cuisine - the colors, the
flavors, the sight of delishious dishes, the fragrance of spices roasting in oils -
readily captivate everyone. Housewives pass down their recipes and culinary
skills from generation to generation. They prepare fresh dishes for every
meal of the day, making sure that the meal’s colors and flavors harmonize.
Their job is made easy by the large variety of available vegetables. The set
table pleases the eyes, the palate and the nose. The Indian diet is colorful, its
culinary styles vary according to the region.
The dishes are spiced more lavishly than what the Western palate is
accustomed to, but aren’t neccessarily hoter. Among the numerous spices the
most commonly used are ginger, cumin, coriander, turmeric, asafoetida,
chilli peppers, bay leaves, black peppers, black mustard seeds, fenugreek
leaves, curry leaves, black salt, fennel seeds, saffron, cinnamon, camphor,
cardamom and cloves.
Their eating style is also different than ours: they eat little bits of many
different dishes.
During a festive meal many varieties of dishes are served. They prepare a
variety of vegetables, two or three different kinds of savory snacks and
sweets, as well as a salad. The meal starts with the bitter flavor, since - as
even the Western cooks recognize - the bitter flavor increases the appetite.
This may be a soupy vegetable dish called shukta. Next on the menu is a bean
soup, or dal. They are usually a creamy consistency, thoush sometimes they
may contain chunks of vegetables as well. They are always served with rice,
and often on top of rice. Rice and dal are followed by vegetables. During a
feast many different vegetable dishes are served: first the lighter, cooked or
steamed vegetables, then richer, deep fried vegetables, or vegetables in a
rich, cream based sauce. These dishes are also served with rice and/or
flatbreads. Sometimes the rice that is served with the vegetable is not the
plain rice that is served with the dal but a rice made richer by the addition of
spices, nuts, vegetables and homemade cheese. Next on the menu are savory
snacks, served by chatni sauces and salads. Saucy sweets, followed by dry
sweets finish the meal.

Everyday meals are simpler – such as rice, and dal, and a vegetable dish. If
we want to make it a little more special, we may add a savory snack and a
chutney.
Lunch should be served hot, and on time (when the sun is highest on the
sky). This will ensure the strongest digestion. Meals should be eaten in a
relaxed, pleasant atmosphere. This is just as important for good digestion as
the quality of the meal. .
According to the Vedic culture, a meal should be offered to God before the
family starts eating. The food thus offered is considered spiritual in nature,
granting long life and health, and purifying the mind and the consciousness.
It is said that in old times the head of the family would open the door
before each meal and loudly yell, „Whoever is hungry should come and eat!”.
The family only ate if noone came, or if the guests had eaten to their
satisfaction.
„Foods dear to those in the mode of goodness increase the duration of life,
purify one’s existence and give strength, health, happiness and satisfaction.
Such foods are juicy, fatty, wholesome, and pleasing to the heart.” /Bhagavad
Gita 17.8/

Soups
In India, dry peas and beans, as well as soups cooked with them are called dal, and
they are always featured as part of a main meal. Dals are rich in iron and vitamin B,
and represent the main source of protein in Vedic meals, where they are traditionally
paired with grains, seeds, nuts, or milk products to allow our bodies to fully absorb
the nutrition they offer.

Mung Dal
Preparation time: 30 minutes
Ingredients:
150 g split mung beans
1 teaspoon turmeric
1-2 tablespoons ghee or oil
2 teaspoons cumin
1 tablespoon grated ginger root
4-5 curry leaves
a pinch of chili powder
¼ teaspoon asafoetida
2 ½ teaspoons salt
a handful of fresh cilantro, chopped
Place the washed mung beans and the turmeric in a heavy bottomed
saucepan with 700 ml water. Bring to a boil and simmer for approximately 30

minutes, or until the beans fall apart and turn creamy.
Heat the ghee or oil in a small frying pan and sauté the cumin seeds until
they turn fragrant. Add the grated ginger and the curry leaves and fry for
another 30 seconds (or until the curry leaves turn a darker shade). Finally,
add the asafoetida and the chili powder, fry for a few moments, then pour
the seasonings into the cooked dal.
Season the soup with salt, bring it to a boil, simmer for two minutes, then
remove it from the heat and garnish it with the chopped herbs.
Balances all three doshas. Pitta types may eat it with yogurt.

Spinach Soup
Preparation: 20 minutes
Serves 4
Ingredients:
400 g spinach
2 tablespoons ghee or oil
2 teaspoons black mustard seeds
1 ½ teaspoon cumin
½ tablespoon minced fresh ginger
½ teaspoon asafoetida
1 ½ teaspoon salt
150 ml cream
Wash the spinach well, and then chop it coarsely.
Heat the ghee or oil in a heavy bottomed pan and sauté the black mustard
seeds until they finish popping. Add the cumin seeds. When they turn
fragrant, stir in the fresh, minced ginger and the asafoetida. Fry for a few
seconds, then add the spinach and cook till it wilts. Add 650 ml water and
bring it to a boil.
Blend, using a blender or a stick blender, then add the salt and the cream.
Return to the flame and simmer for 2-3 minutes.
Reduces kapha. Vata types enjoy in moderation. Not recommended for pitta types,
because spinach aggravates pitta.

Karhi
Preparation: 35 minutes
Ingredients:
For the karhi:
300 ml yogurt
600 ml water
3 tablespoons chickpea flour
½ teaspoon turmeric
2 teaspoons salt
2 tablespoons ghee or oil
1 teaspoon black mustard seeds
1,5 teaspoon cumin
6 curry leaves
½ tablespoon grated fresh ginger
2-3 dried chillies, crushed
¼ teaspoon asafoetida
2 teaspoons sugar

For the pakoras:
100 g chickpea flour
1 teaspoon salt
½ teaspoon baking powder
water
oil for deep-frying
Mix the yogurt with the chickpea flour and whisk them to a smooth paste.
Add the water and the turmeric and whisk again to make a smooth batter.
Heat the ghee or oil. Sauté the black mustard seeds in the hot oil. When
they stop popping, add the cumin seeds. Once the cumin seeds are fragrant,
add the ginger, crushed red chilies and curry leaves. After 30 seconds, add
the asafoetida. Stir to mix, then pour the chickpea batter in the spices.
Season the mix with salt and sugar. Bring it to a boil, stirring often, then turn
the flame to medium low and let it simmer for 6-8 minutes.
To prepare the pakoras, mix the chickpea flour with the salt and the baking
powder, then whisk in the water to get a thick, smooth, pancake-like batter.
Heat the oil for deep-frying to 350 F or 180 C. Drop teaspoons of dough into
the hot oil. Fry the dumplings to an even golden brown color.
Mix the pakoras into the karhi just a few minutes before serving.
Suitable for people with pitta or vatta constitutions. Not recommended for people
with kapha dosha.

Carrot Soup
Preparation: 35 minutes
Ingredients:
3-4 carrots, cleaned and diced
1 tablespoon ghee or oil
1 teaspoon cumin powder
1 teaspoon ground ginger
a pinch of cayenne pepper (to taste)
150 ml cream
a pinch of ground black pepper
2 teaspoons salt
a handful of chopped fresh coriander leaves
Boil the carrots in a small amount of water till soft. Blend.
Heat the ghee or oil in a small frying pan. Stir the spices into the warm oil,
then pour the flavored oil over the carrot puree.
Add the cream and enough water to get a consistency that is to your liking.

Season with salt and pepper. Bring the soup to a simmer, then immediately
remove from the heat.
Garnish with chopped coriander.
Suitable for vata and kapha dosha. Individuals with kapha constitution consume in
moderation.

Red Lentil Soup with Ginger and
Lemon
Preparation: 30 minutes
Ingredients:
150 g red lentils
2 tablespoons ghee or oil
1 teaspoon black mustard seeds
1 teaspoon cumin
1 tablespoon minced fresh ginger
6-8 curry leaves

a pinch of cayenne pepper (to taste)
½ teaspoon asafoetida
½ teaspoon turmeric
a handful of fresh coriander leaves, chopped
½ teaspoon lemon juice
2 ½ teaspoons salt
Wash the lentils. Bring 700 ml water to a boil, then add the cleaned lentils.
Cook until the lentils are soft and falling apart, then prepare the spice mix.
Heat the ghee or oil in a small, heavy bottomed saucepan. Sauté the black
mustard seeds in the hot oil. Once they stop popping, add the cumin, fry for
30 seconds, then stir in the ginger and the curry leaves. Fry them for another
30 seconds, and then add cayenne pepper, asafoetida and turmeric in quick
succession. Stir to combine. Add the spice mixture to the cooked lentils.
The soup should have a thick, creamy soup consistency. You may need to
add a little water if it is too thick. Season with salt, bring to a simmer, then
remove from the heat. Stir in the lemon juice and garnish with coriander
leaves.
Decreases vata and kapha, but increases pitta.
„The three doshas - vata, pitta and kapha - in their natural states nourish the
body; in an imbalanced state they destroy the body.” (Astanga Hridaya)

Rice
Rice is one of the basic elements of Indian cuisine. It is a versatile grain that can be
prepared in a seemingly endless variety of ways. Simple, steamed rice is a perfect
accompaniment to everyday meals. On special days we can enrich our rice dish with
spices, vegetables, yogurt and even homemade cheese.

Kitchari
Preparation: 45 minutes
Ingredients:
200 ml mung dal
2 tablespoons ghee or oil
3 teaspoon cumin
2 cloves
a small cinnamon stick
1 tablespoon grated ginger
2 bay leaves
½ teaspoon asafoetida
a pinch of chilli powder (to taste and according to one’s dosha)
¾ teaspoon turmeric
200 g mixed vegetables (carrots, zucchini, bell peppers, green peas,
string beans, etc, to suit your dosha)
3 teaspoons salt

a handful of coriander leaves, minced
½ cup yogurt, for serving
Wash the mung dal well. Bring 600 ml water to boil. Add the dal.
Clean and dice the vegetables.
Heat the ghee or oil in a medium pan, sauté the cumin seeds until they turn
fragrant, then add the bay leaf, the grated ginger, and the cinnamon stick.
After a few seconds, stir in the asafoetida, the chili powder and the turmeric.
Add the vegetables, stir well to mix with the spices, then add enough water
to cover the vegetables.
Bring to a boil, simmer for ten minutes, then add the rice and simmer until
the rice is soft. By now the dal should be cooked as well – the beans should
fall apart and look pudding-like. Mix it to the rice and vegetables and season
with salt. Boil for another three minutes. If it appears too dry, add enough
water to get a stew-like consistency.
Finally, garnish with coriander leaves. Serve with yogurt.
Suitable for all three doshas, but kapha types should not eat it with yogurt.

Rice with Mint
Preparation time: 20 minutes
Ingredients:
200 g rice
6 mint leaves, minced
a handful of coriander leaves, minced
2 tablespoons fresh grated coconut
400 ml water
1 ½ teaspoons salt
2 tablespoons ghee or oil
1 teaspoon cumin
2 cloves
Blend the mint and the coriander leaves with the coconut and 50 ml water.
Bring 400 ml water to a quick boil with the salt.
In a separate saucepan, heat the ghee or oil, sauté the cumin seeds and the
cloves until they turn fragrant. Add the rice, and sauté on a low flame for

about four minutes, or until it gives off a deep, nutty aroma.
Add the herbed coconut paste and the hot water. Cover tightly and cook
over the smallest flame until the rice grains are cooked, or about 12 minutes.
Suitable for all three doshas.

Tomato Rice
Preparation time: 20 minutes
Ingredients:
400 ml water
1 ½ teaspoons salt
½ teaspoon turmeric
2 tablespoons ghee or oil
2 cardamom pods
1 stick cinnamon
¼ teaspoon asafoetida
6 cashews
1 large tomato, grated
200 g rice
a tablespoon of minced coriander leaves
Bring 400 ml water to a rapid boil with the salt and the turmeric.
In a separate pan, heat the ghee or oil, add the spices, the cashew nuts and

the rice. Sautee to lightly toast the grains and the nuts. Add the boiling hot
water and the grated tomato.
Cover tightly, reduce the heat to low and cook till the rice is tender.
Suitable for vata and dosha types, but not recommended to pitta types.

Vegetable rice
Preparation time: 20 minutes
Ingredients:
200 g rice
2 tablespoons ghee or oil
1 teaspoon black mustard seeds
1 teaspoon cumin
1 cardamom pod
1 teaspoon grated ginger root
2 bay leaves
a pinch of asafoetida
¼ teaspoon turmeric
120 g mixed vegetables (zucchini, green beans and green peas)
400 ml water
1 ½ teaspoons salt

a tablespoon of minced coriander leaves
Heat the ghee or oil in a heavy bottomed pan. Add the mustard seeds. When
they start popping, add the cumin seeds, sauté for 30 second, then add the
cardamom pods, the minced ginger and the bay leaf. Once those turn
fragrant, add the asafoetida and the turmeric. Stir, add the vegetables, and
sauté, stirring, for three or four minutes.
Meanwhile, boil the water.
Add the rice to the vegetables, toast for two minutes, then carefully pour
the boiling water over the mix. Cover with a tight fitting lid and steam on a
low flame until the rice is tender. Garnish with coriander leaves.
Suitable for all three doshas.

Vegetable Pulao
Ingredients:
2 tablespoons ghee or oil
10 g mixed vegetables (carrots, green beans, cauliflower, green peas)
400 ml water
1 1/2 teaspoons salt
egy stick cinnamon
2 cloves
1 tablespoon cashew nuts
200 g rice
Bring the water to a rapid boil. Add the salt.
Meanwhile, sauté the vegetables in a heavy bottomed pan for 4-5 minutes.
Add the spices and the nuts, sauté for another two minutes, then add the
boiling water.
Cover the pot with a tight fitting lid, lower the flame and then cook until
the grains are tender, about 12 minutes.
Suitable for all three doshas.
recipe_name: about four minutes, or until it gives off a deep, nutty aroma.

text:
Saffron Rice
Preparation: 20 minutes
Ingredients:
4-5 strands of saffron
1 tablespoon warm water
400 ml water
1 1/2 teaspoons salt
2 tablespoons ghee or oil
3 bay leaves
a small stick of cinnamon
4 cloves
200 g rice
Soak the saffron in a tablespoon of warm water.
Bring the water to a rapid boil with the salt.
Meanwhile, sauté the rice and the spices in the ghee or oil. When the grains
smell slightly toasted, carefully add the hot water and the saffron. Cover with
a tight fitting lid and lower the flame. Cook till the rice is tender, or about 12
minutes.
Pacifies vata and kapha doshas, but pitta types should consume in moderation.
Ayurveda considers spices a subtle type of food. The regular consumption of
spices is recommended for everyone to provide nourishment on a subtle level.

Main Courses
Indian vegetable dishes transport the lovers of vegetarian food to heaven. These
dishes are unsurpassed in the world, whether fried, boiled, steamed, sautéed, dry or
gravy based. In the following collection you will find everyday dishes as well as ones
that are fit to be served at a feast. These recipes will prove to you that humble
vegetables can become gourmet delicacies if one knows how to use the right spices.

Cabbage and Green Peas
Preparation: 35 minutes
Ingredients:
3 tablespoons ghee or oil
2 teaspoons cumin
1 green chili, minced (or to taste)
1 tablespoon grated fresh ginger
1 1/2 teaspoons coriander powder
½ teaspoon turmeric
2 medium potatoes
600 g cabbage
200 g green peas
1 large tomato
½ teaspoon garam masala
2 teaspoons salt
Cook the green peas. Meanwhile, prepare the vegetables: peel and cube the

potatoes, slice the cabbage, and chop the tomato.
Heat the oil or ghee in a large wok. Fry the cumin seeds until they turn
fragrant, then add the ginger and the green chili. When the chili is wilted,
stir in the coriander powder and the turmeric. Stir well, and add the
potatoes.
Cook, covered, stirring often. After ten minutes, add the cabbage. Continue
cooking, adjusting the flame in a way that allows the cabbage to caramelize
slightly. Once the potatoes are soft, add the green peas, the tomatoes, the
garam masala, and the salt. Continue to cook, this time without a lid, for
another 2-3 minutes.
Suitable for kapha and pitta types, but not recomended for vata types.

Stir-Fried Bitter Melon
Preparation: 25 minutes
Ingredients:
800 g bitter melon
3 tablespoons ghee or oil
1 teaspoon black mustard seeds
2 teaspoons cumin
1 tablespoon grated ginger root
1/3 teaspoon asafoetida
½ teaspoon turmeric
1 tablespoon minced coriander leaves
the juice of half a lime
1 1/2 teaspoons salt
Bitter melon is a cooling vegetable. It is easy to digest, and calms kapha and
pitta.

Cut the bitter melons into thin slices.
Heat the ghee or oil in a frying pan. Once the fat is hot, add the black
mustard seeds. When the seeds stop crackling, add the cumin seeds and the
ginger, and sauté until the cumin seeds turn fragrant. Stir in the powdered
spices, closely followed by the bitter melon slices.
Stir-fry for a minute, season with salt, and cover with a lid. Continue
cooking on a low flame, stirring often, for a further 15-20 minutes, or until
the vegetable is soft. Remove from the flame, and sprinkle with the lime
juice.
Reduces kapha. Pitta may eat it in moderation . Not recommended for vatta.

Okra and Potatoes
Preparation: 30 minutes
Ingredients:
600 g okra
2 medium potatoes
2 tablespoons ghee or oil
2 teaspoons cumin
1 tablespoon grated fresh ginger root
¼ teaspoon asafoetida
2 teaspoons coriander powder
a pinch of chilli powder
2 medium tomatoes, grated
1 1/2 teaspoons salt
Clean and dice the vegetables.
Heat the ghee or oil in a frying pan. Add the cumin seeds. Once they are
fragrant, add the grated ginger. A few seconds later, stir in the powdered
spices, closely followed by the diced vegetables.

Sautee for a minute or two, then add the tomatoes and enough water to just
cover the vegetables. Cook on a high flame without a lid, until the vegetables
become soft and the water is mostly evaporated.
Suitable for kapha and pitta, vata consume in moderation.

Cauliflower-Green Pea Masala
Preparation: 40 minutes
Ingredients:
3 tablespoons oil
4 tablespoons fresh, grated coconut
1 teaspoon powdered ginger
a handful of coriander leaves, minced
¾ teaspoon turmeric
2 teaspoons coriander powder
1 1/2 teaspoons cumin
½ teaspoon asafoetida
1 cauliflower
300 g green peas
1 medium tomato, chopped
2 papadums (optional)

2 teaspoons salt
First, make a spice paste: blend the shredded coconut, the ginger, the
coriander leaves, the turmeric, and the coriander powder with a cup of water
until smooth.
Heat the ghee or oil in a heavy bottomed frying pan. Add the cumin seeds
and fry them until they turn fragrant. Stir in the asafetida, then, after a few
seconds, sprinkle in the chili powder, closely followed by the vegetables. Fry
them for a minute, then add enough water to just cover the vegetables.
Season with salt, and cook until the vegetables are tender. Remove from the
flame, and crumble two papadums into the dish.
Serve with rice.
Reduces pitta and kapha. Not recomended for vata.

Alu-Gobi
Preparation: 30 minutes
Ingredients:
1000 g potatoes and cauliflower, mixed
3 tablespoons ghee or oil
2 teaspoons cumin
1 tablespoon grated fresh ginger root
5 curry leaves
½ teaspoon asafoetida
a pinch of chilli powder
½ teaspoon turmeric
1 medium tomato, chopped
2 teaspoons salt
¾ teaspoon garam masala
1 bunch coriander leaves
Peel and dice the potatoes. Separate the cauliflower into small rosettes.

Heat the ghee or oil in a large frying pan or wok. Fry the cumin until
fragrant, then add the ginger and the curry leaves. Fry them for five seconds,
then add the asafetida and turmeric, immediately followed by the tomato.
Sautee for a minute, or until the tomato softens, then add the potatoes and
cauliflower. Add ½ cup of water, season with salt, cover with a lid, and cook
until the vegetables are tender.
Add the garam masala and garnish with coriander leaves. Mix well and
remove from the flame.
Suitable for all three doshas.

Green Beans in Fragrant Coconut
Gravy
Preparation: 35 minutes
Ingredients:
2 tablespoons coconut oil or other oil
2 teaspoons black mustard seeds
6-8 curry leaves
2 tablespoons shredded coconut (fresh or dry)
1 tablespoon grated fresh ginger root
2 teaspoons coriander powder
¼ teaspoon ground chilli peppers (to taste)
½ teaspoon turmeric
700 g green beans
1 1/2 teaspoons salt
150 ml coconut cream
recipe_name: First, make a spice paste: blend the shredded coconut, the ginger, the

text:
Heat the ghee or oil in a heavy bottomed frying pan. Add the mustard seeds.
When they start crackling, add the curry leaves, the ginger and the shredded
coconut. Once the coconut smells aromatic, add the coriander and chili
powders. Fry, stirring, for 5 seconds, then add the turmeric and the washed,
chopped green beans. Season with salt, and add enough water to cover the
vegetables.
Cover with a lid and cook until the green beans are soft. Add the coconut
paste, stir well to make sure it is well distributed, and cook for a few more
minutes without the lid to thicken the sauce.
Suitable for all three doshas.

Potatoes in Creamy Coconut Sauce
Preparation: 35 minutes
Ingredients:
800 g potatoes, peeled and diced
3 tablespoons fresh grated coconut
150 ml water
3 tablespoons ghee or oil
1 teaspoon black mustard seeds
4 curry leaves
1 tablespoon grated fresh ginger root
1 teaspoon ajwain
½ teaspoon asafoetida
½ teaspoon turmeric
1 tomato, diced
1 teaspoon garam masala
2 teaspoons salt
Make a spice mixture by blending the coriander leaves, the coconut and the

water to a smooth paste.
Heat the ghee or oil in a heavy bottomed frying pan or wok. Add the
mustard seeds. Once the seeds stop crackling, add the curry leaves, the
ginger and the ajwain seeds, fry them for 5 seconds, then sprinkle in the
asafoetida and the turmeric, followed by the spice paste. Fry for a minute,
then add the potatoes and the tomato. Season with salt, cover with a lid, and
cook until the potato is soft. Stir in the garam masala and remove from the
flame.
Suitable for vata and kapha. Pita may eat it in moderation.

Spiced Butternut Squash
Preparation: 25 minutes
Ingredients:
2 tablespoons ghee or oil
1 teaspoon black mustard seeds
2 teaspoons cumin
6 curry leaves
½ teaspoon asafoetida
a pinch of chilli powder
½ teaspoon turmeric
800 g pumpkin, peeled and diced
200 ml water
2 teaspoons salt
a handful of coriander leaves, minced
Heat the ghee or oil in a heavy bottomed frying pan or wok. Add the black
mustard seeds. Once the seeds stop crackling, add the cumin seeds and the
curry leaves. Once the spices turn aromatic, stir in the asafoetida, the chili
powder and the turmeric powder, fry them for a few seconds, and then add
the cubed butternut squash. Stir well, add water, and simmer, covered, until
the squash is tender. Remove from the flame and garnish with chopped
coriander leaves.
Suitable for vata and kapha. Pitta may consume it in moderation.
recipe_name: Heat the ghee or oil in a heavy bottomed frying pan. Add the mustard seeds.

text:
Stir Fried Vegetables
Preparation: 30 minutes
Ingredients:
1000 g mixed vegetables, cleaned and diced
3 tablespoons ghee or oil
1,5 teaspoon cumin
2,5 teaspoons coriander powder
½ teaspoon ground chilli peppers
½ teaspoon turmeric
½ teaspoon asafoetida
1 teaspoon ground ginger
2,5 teaspoons salt

¼ c water
a small handful coriander leaves, minced
Use any combination of vegetables, such as potatoes, beetroots, cabbage, bell
peppers, carrots, winter squash, zucchini, spinach, cauliflower, baby corn,
broccoli, green beans, green peas. I recommend that you choose seasonal
vegetables that are compatible with your doshas.
Heat the ghee or oil in a wok or a large frying pan. Fry the cumin seeds
until they are fragrant. Add all of the other spices, closely followed by the
vegetables. Add ¼ cup water, season with salt, cover with a lid and simmer on
medium large flame. Stir often, but allow the vegetables to get caramelized a
little. Once they are tender, remove from the flame and stir in the coriander
leaves.
Suitable for all three doshas.

Stuffed Zucchini
Preparation: 40 minutes
Ingredients:
2 medium zucchinis
2 tablespoons ghee or oil
2 teaspoons coriander powder
1 teaspoon cumin powder
½ teaspoon asafoetida
½ teaspoon turmeric

a pinch of chilli powder
¼ teaspoon amchoor (dry mango powder)
4 tablespoons fresh grated coconut
a big handful of coriander leaves
1 teaspoon salt
Slice the zucchinis in half, and, with the help of a melon baller or a small
spoon, scrape out the flesh, leaving a ½ inch thick shell. Mince the removed
flesh.
Heat the ghee or oil in a heavy bottomed pan. Add the coriander powder,
cumin powder, asafetida, turmeric, chili and amchoor powders, followed by
the fresh, grated coconut. Fry until the coconut smells aromatic. Add the
minced zucchini flesh, season with salt and cook for another 4-5 minutes. Fill
the zucchini shells with this mixture, and bake at 375 F for 15-20 minutes.
Suitable for all three doshas.

Vegetables Cooked in Milk
Preparation: 40 minutes
Ingredients:
1000 g vegetables (carrots, cauliflower, green beans and green peas)
2 tablespoons ghee or oil
2 teaspoons cumin
1 teaspoon coriander powder
½ teaspoon asafoetida
½ teaspoon turmeric
200 ml full fat milk
2 teaspoons ground black mustard seeds
2 teaspoons salt
a handful of coriander leaves, minced
Clean and dice the vegetables. Heat the ghee or oil in a heavy bottomed pot.
Fry the cumin seeds until they are fragrant, add the coriander powder, the

asafetida and the turmeric, closely followed by the vegetables. Add 150 ml
water, season with salt, and simmer, covered, on medium flame.
Meanwhile, mix the ground black mustard seeds into 200 ml milk.
When the vegetables are nearly cooked, add the flavored milk. Once the
vegetables are tender, remove the pot from the flame and garnish your
vegetables with coriander leaves.
All three doshas should consume in moderation.

Paneer in Fragrant Tomato Gravy
Preparation: 30 minutes
Ingredients:
400 g paneer
4 tomatoes
8 cashews
2 tablespoons ghee or oil
2 teaspoons cumin
1 tablespoon grated fresh ginger root
a pinch of chilli powder
½ teaspoon turmeric
150 ml cream
2 teaspoons salt
1 teaspoon cane sugar
½ teaspoon garam masala
a handful of minced coriander leaves
Cut the paneer into ½ inch cubes. Blend the tomatoes smooth with the
cashew nuts.
Heat the ghee or oil in a heavy bottomed pot. Add the cumin seeds and fry
them until they are fragrant. Add the ginger, fry for 5 seconds, then stir in
the chili powder and the turmeric. Add the tomato-cashew mixture and cook,
stirring often, until somewhat thickened. Add 150 ml water and 150 ml
cream. Season with salt and sugar and bring it to a boil. Add the paneer cubes
and simmer for 3 minutes. Stir in the garam masala and the coriander leaves
and remove from the flame.
Suitable for vata. Kapha and pitta consume in moderation .

Palak Paneer
Preparation: 25 minutes
Ingredients:
200 g paneer
400 g spinach
2 tablespoons ghee or oil
1 teaspoon cumin
1 tablespoon grated fresh ginger root
1 1/2 teaspoons coriander powder
½ teaspoon turmeric
100 ml cream
1 teaspoon salt
½ teaspoon garam masala
Cut the paneer into ½ inch cubes. Wash the spinach well in cold water to
make sure it is very clean. Chop it small.
Heat the ghee or oil in a heavy bottomed pan, add the cumin seeds and fry
them until fragrant. Add the ginger, fry for half a minute, then add the

powdered coriander and the turmeric, immediately followed by the spinach.
Sautee for 6-8 minutes, or until the spinach wilts.
Add the cream, season with salt, and simmer for 3 minutes. Stir in the
garam masala and remove from the flame.
Suitable for all three doshas.
