text:
Mixed Vegetable Curry
Preparation: 35 minutes
Ingredients:
2 tablespoons ghee or oil
2 teaspoons cumin
1 tablespoon grated fresh ginger root
1 green chilli peppers (to taste)
½ teaspoon asafoetida
¾ teaspoon turmeric
2,5 teaspoons coriander powder
4-5 medium tomatoes
1000 g mixed vegetables (such as cauliflower, green beans, green peas,
sweet corn, zucchinis, brussel sprouts, broccoli, carrots)
2,5 teaspoons salt
1 teaspoon sugar
1 teaspoon garam masala
a handful of coriander leaves, minced
Wash and dice the vegetables. Puree or grate the tomato.
Heat the ghee or oil in a heavy bottomed pot. Add the cumin seeds and fry
them until they turn fragrant. Add the ginger and green chilies. Fry them for
half a minute, then add the asafetida, the turmeric and the coriander
powder, followed by the tomato. Fry for a minute, then add the vegetables
and enough water to barely cover them. Season with salt and sugar, and cook
on high flame until the vegetables are soft, and most of the water is
evaporated. Add the garam masala and the coriander leaves and remove
from the flame.
Suitable for all three doshas.

Palak Chole
Preparation: 20 minutes
Ingredients:
3 tablespoons oil
2 teaspoons cumin
1 tablespoon fresh grated ginger
1-2 green chillies, minced (or crushed red chillies)
2 teaspoons coriander powder
½ teaspoon asafoetida
1 teaspoon turmeric
200 ml tomato puree (or 3 tomatoes, grated or blended)
400 g spinach (fresh or frozen)
2 teaspoons salt
1 teaspoon sugar
200 g cooked chickpeas
¾ teaspoon garam masala
Heat the ghee or oil in a heavy bottomed pot. Add the cumin seeds. Once they
turn fragrant, add the ginger and the chili peppers. Sautee for 30 seconds,
then add the coriander powder, the asafetida and the turmeric. Stir once,
then add the tomato puree. Simmer till thickened, then add 150-200 ml
water. Season with salt and sugar. Bring to a boil, add the spinach and cook
for about 5 minutes, until the spinach wilts.
Add the cooked chickpeas and the garam masala. Continue to simmer for 4-
5 minutes, then remove from the fire.
Serve with rice.
Suitable for kapha and vata types. Pitta types consume in moderation.

Potato-Green Bean Charchari
Preparation: 50 minutes
Ingredients:
5 tablespoon ghee or oil
½ teaspoon asafoetida
6 curry leaves
1 green chilli peppers
¾ teaspoon turmeric
600 g potatoes
400 g green beans
¼ teaspoon ground black peppers
2 teaspoons salt
a handful of coriander leaves, minced
Peel and dice the potatoes. Trim the green beans and cut them to 1 ½ inch
pieces. Mince the green chili.
Heat the ghee or oil in a wok. Add the asafetida and the green chili. Fry for

half a minute, then add the curry leaves, and then a few seconds later the
turmeric. Stir in the potatoes and the green beans, and enough water to
barely cover the vegetables. Season with salt and top with torn basil leaves.
Cook on medium high flame. Do not stir. Be patient, let all the water boil
away, and let the vegetables caramelize and slightly stick to the bottom.
Remove from the flame, add the coriander leaves and cover with a lid. Let it
stand for five minutes, then gently stir to mix.
Suitable for all three doshas, but pitta should use less chili or leave it out altogether.

Brussel Sprout Masala
Preparation: 35 minutes.
Ingredients:
2 tablespoons ghee or oil
1 teaspoon black mustard seeds
1 ½ teaspoons cumin
5-6 curry leaves
½ teaspoon asafoetida
1 ½ teaspoons coriander powder
¾ teaspoon turmeric
a pinch of chilli powder (to taste)
3 tomatoes, grated
600 g brussel sprouts
1 ½ teaspoons salt
Wash and trim the Brussels sprouts. Cut the larger ones in half.
Heat the ghee or oil in a heavy bottomed pan. Add the black mustard seeds.

When they stop crackling, add the cumin seeds and the curry leaves. Once
they are fragrant, add the asafetida, turmeric, coriander powder and chili
powder. Stir for a few seconds, then add the grated tomatoes and the
Brussels sprouts. Add enough water to almost cover the vegetables. Season
with salt and cook till the Brussels sprouts are tender and the water has
evaporated.
Suitable for pitta and kapha types. Increases vata dosha.

Zucchini Sauteed with Spices and
Coconut
Preparation: 20 minutes
Ingredients:
2 tablespoons ghee or oil
1 teaspoon black mustard seeds
2 teaspoons cumin
5-6 curry leaves
1 tablespoon shredded coconut
a pinch of chilli powder
½ teaspoon asafoetida
½ teaspoon turmeric
800 g zucchini
1 ½ teaspoons salt
Dice the zucchini into small cubes.
Heat the ghee or oil in a wok or large frying pan. Toss in the mustard seeds.
When they start crackling, add the cumin seeds and fry for 30 seconds, until
they turn fragrant. Add the curry leaves and the shredded coconut. Fry till
the coconut is slightly toasted. Sprinkle with the chili powder and stir in the
zucchini. Stir-fry for another 8-10 minutes, or until the vegetable is cooked,
but still firm. Stir occasionally, but let the cubes get caramelized a little bit.
Decreases kapha and pitta doshas. Vata types consume in moderation.

Sweet Potatoes with Sweet Spices
Preparation: 30 minutes.
Ingredients:
2 tablespoons ghee or oil
1 ½ teaspoons black mustard seedss
5-6 curry leaves
2 cloves
a small piece of cinnamon stick
½ teaspoon asafoetida
½ teaspoon turmeric
1 ½ teaspoons coriander powder
a pinch of chilli powder
800 g peeled, diced sweet potatoes
200 ml water
2 teaspoons salt
a handful of coriander leaves, minced

Heat the ghee or oil in a heavy bottomed pan. Toss in the black mustard
seeds. Once they stop crackling, add the curry leaves, the cinnamon stick and
the cloves. Fry for 30 seconds, then sprinkle in the asafetida, the turmeric,
the coriander powder and the chili powder. Stir to mix, add the sweet
potatoes and sauté them with the spices for a minute or two. Add enough
water to cover the vegetable, season with salt, and cook, covered, until the
sweet potatoes are tender. Remove from the flame and fold in the coriander
leaves.
Reduces vata dosha. Suitable for pitta types. Kapha types consume in moderation.

Baby Corn with Bell Pepper
Preparation: 40 minutes
Ingredients:
15-20 baby corn
2 tomatoes
1 bell pepper
2 tablespoons ghee or oil
2 teaspoons cumin
a pinch of chilli powder
½ teaspoon turmeric
2 teaspoons salt
a handful of coriander leaves, minced
Boil the baby corn till tender.
Meanwhile, grate or blend the tomatoes and dice the pepper.
Heat the ghee or oil in a heavy bottomed frying pan and sauté the cumin
seeds until they turn a shade darker and are fragrant. Sprinkle in the chili

powder and the turmeric, immediately followed by the diced pepper. Fry for
a minute, then add 200 ml water and cook for 10 minutes. Season with salt,
add the drained baby corn and cook for another 3-4 minutes. Remove from
the flame and fold in the coriander leaves.
Suitable for vata and kapha types. Pitta types consume in moderation .

Paneer Jalfrezi
Preparation: 30 minutes
Ingredients:
2 tablespoons ghee or oil
2 teaspoons cumin
½ teaspoon grated fresh ginger root
1 teaspoon kalonji seeds
½ teaspoon asafoetida
a pinch of chilli powder
½ teaspoon turmeric
250 g green beans
1 medium carrot
1 bell pepper
1 large tomato, grated
2 teaspoons salt

200 g paneer, diced
½ teaspoon garam masala
a handful of coriander leaves, minced
Wash and dice the vegetables. Grate or blend the tomato.
Heat the ghee or oil in a heavy bottomed frying pan over medium fire.
Sautee the cumin seeds until darkened and aromatic. Add the ginger and the
kalonji seeds, fry for another 30 seconds, then sprinkle in the asafetida, chili
powder and the turmeric. Stir to mix, then add the vegetables and sauté for
2-3 minutes. Add the blended tomato and enough water to just cover the
vegetables. Season with salt and cook on a large flame until the vegetables
are tender and the water has evaporated. Carefully fold in the paneer pieces,
the garam masala and the coriander leaves.
Suitable for all three doshas.

Rajma – Creamy Kidney Bean Soup
Preparation: 90 minutes to cook the beans + 30 minutes
Ingredients:
3 tablespoons ghee or oil
1 tablespoon grated fresh ginger root
a cinnamon stick
2 cloves
2 bay leaves
1 cardamom pod
2 teaspoons dried fenugreek leaves
2 teaspoons coriander powder
¼ teaspoon ground chilli peppers
3 tomatoes, grated
500 g kidney beans
3 tablespoons cream
2 teaspoons salt
½ teaspoon garam masala

Wash and soak the kidney beans for 8 hours, or overnight. Strain, cover with
fresh water in a heavy bottomed pot, and cook till very soft.
Grate or blend the tomatoes.
Heat the ghee or oil in a heavy bottomed pan. Add the ginger, the
cinnamon stick, the cloves, the cardamom pod and the the bay leaves. Sautee
these spices for 30 seconds, then sprinkle in the coriander powder and the
red chili powder, followed by the blended tomatoes. Cook till the tomatoes
thicken to a paste. Add the cooked beans, 150 ml water, and the cream.
Season with salt. Bring to a simmer, simmer for 3 minutes, then stir in the
garam masala and remove from the flame.
Suitable for pitta and kapha types, vata types consume in moderation.
Besides diet and herbs, Ayurveda utilizes yoga, meditation, oil massage,
aromatherapy and the healing power of prescious stones to balance the doshas.
Flavors influence our emotions. Sweet flavors nourish love, savory greed, sour
envy, bitter pain, hot hatred, astringent fear.
Certain herbal teas are suitable for all three doshas. Such herbs include
peppermint, spearmint, fennel and chamomile.

Breads
Instead of our common yeasted, sliced bread, India’s staple is freshly prepared flat
bread and its variations, prepared with whole meal flour. Most of them use little more
than flour, water and salt, yet are fragrant, scrumptious and nourishing.

Chapati
Preparation: 45 minutes
Ingredients:
100 g all purpose flour
150 g whole meal flour
1 1/2 teaspoons salt
about 150 ml warm water
butter for brushing

Combine the flours and the salt, then slowly add enough warm water to make
a smooth, soft dough. Knead well, place it in a bowl and cover with a damp
kitchen towel. Let it rest for at least 15 minutes, or up to two hours for even
better results.
Divide the dough into 15 patties. Roll out each one of them into round, thin
circles.
Heat a cast iron, low rimmed pan over medium high fire. Once hot,
carefully place a chapatti onto the pan. As soon as you see small bubbles on
the top, flip it over, and start gently pressing on the top with the flat of a
spatula. This will help the chapattis inflate. Once they balloon, remove them
from the pan. Brush both sides with melted butter and serve hot.
Suitable for all three doshas.

Tomato Puri
Preparation time: 30 minutes
Ingredients:
250 g flour (all purpose and whole meal, mixed)
2 tablespoons sesame oil
1 1/2 teaspoons salt
a handful of spinach leaves, chopped
½ teaspoon turmeric
1 tomato, grated
ghee or oil for deep-frying
Combine the flour and salt. Add the oil and rub it in with your fingers. Add
the spinach, turmeric and grated or blended tomato. Slowly knead in enough
water to make a pliable dough. Let it rest for 15 minutes, or up to two hours.
Pinch walnut size pieces out of the dough, and roll them into thin and
smooth disks.
Heat ghee or oil in a wok or deep-frying pan. Carefully lower a puri into the
fat. Once it rises to the surface, gently push it down under the surface with a
slotted spoon. Repeat this until it inflates, then continue frying until the
bottom side turns golden brown. Turn it over and fry the other side. Drain in
a colander or on paper towels.
Suitable for vata types. Increases pitta and kapha doshas.

Tava Naan
Preparation: 45 minutes
Naan is a popular flat bread in India. It is traditionally baked in a tandoor
oven. This recipe is for those that don’t own a tandoor oven – they can still
enjoy naan, baked on a cast iron pan.
Ingredients:
200 g all purpose flour
100 g whole meal flour
1 1/2 teaspoons salt
2 tablespoons oil
3 tablespoons yogurt
1 ts dried yeast
Blend the flours, the yeast and the salt. Rub in the butter, then add the
yogurt and enough lukewarm water to make a soft, but not sticky dough.
Knead well. Cover and let it stand for 30 minutes.

Divide the dough into 6 pieces, shape them into patties and roll them into
3-4 mm thick disks.
Heat a cast iron, low rimmed pan over medium high flame. Carefully place
a naan on the hot pan. Bake for a few seconds on the dry pan, then flip the
naan and cover your pan with a lid. This will help the flat bread to become
light and airy. Once the second side is baked, remove from the pan, butter
the top and sprinkle with chopped coriander leaves.
If you are feeling adventurous, you can try baking your naan Indian style:
brush the top of the dough disk with a little water, then place it, wet side
down, on the hot pan. It should get stuck – do not try to move it. After about
two seconds, turn the pan upside down, and hold it above a high flame. It
should quickly develop bubbles. Once it falls off the pan, it is ready!
Suitable for all three doshas.

Masala Paratha
Preparation: 45 minutes
Ingredients:
250 g flour (all purpose and whole meal, mixed)
2 teaspoons salt
1 teaspoon ajwain
½ teaspoon cumin powder
½ teaspoon turmeric
a pinch of asafoetida
1 tablespoon ghee or oil
1 tablespoon cilantro, minced
Combine the flours, the salt and the spices. Add the coriander leaves, the oil,
and enough water to make a soft, pliable dough. Knead well. Cover and let it
rest for at least 15 minutes. Divide into 12 patties, then roll them into thin,
smooth disks. For a flaky texture, lightly brush the surface of the pastry disks
with oil, fold it in half, brush with oil again, and fold in half again. Roll the
resulting triangular shapes thin.
Heat a heavy cast iron pan on medium flame, and fry each side of the
parathas for a minute or two. Serve hot.
Suitable for all three doshas.
Sesame and almond oils are the recommended massage oils for reducing vata.
They are even more potent with the addition of camphor, sandal or cinnamon
essential oils.
Recommended massage oils for reducing pitta: coconut or sunflower oil and
ghee. Recommended essential oils: rose, gardenia, jasmin.
Mustard and flax oil are recommended as massage oils for reducing kapha.
Recommended essential oils are clove, cinnamon and cedar.

Savory Snacks
Savory snacks, prepared with vegetables, milk products, grains and beans, can serve
as a main meal if served with a chutney or a salad. They are visually pleasing dishes,
excellent for entertaining. Some of them are quickly prepared, others take time and
care.

Green Crepes
Preparation: 40 minutes
Ingredients:
200 g chickpea flour
2 teaspoons salt
a pinch of chilli powder
½ teaspoon garam masala
½ tablespoon grated fresh ginger root
water
a handful of fresh spinach leaves
Combine the flour with the salt and the spices. Whisk in enough water to get
a smooth pancake batter like consistency. Finally, fold in the chopped
spinach leaves.
Heat a large diameter frying pan on medium fire. Brush it with oil or
melted butter, then pour a ladleful of batter into the pan. Carefully spread it
to get a thin, round crepe. Fry till the bottom is golden brown, flip it over,
and fry the second side. Serve hot.

Coriander Vada
Preparation: 45 minutes
Ingredients:
2 tablespoons ghee or oil
a bunch of cilantro
1 teaspoon black mustard seeds
2 teaspoons sesame seeds
1 teaspoon cumin powder
1 teaspoon coriander powder
½ teaspoon asafoetida
a pinch of chilli powder (to taste)
200 g chickpea flour
200 ml yogurt
2,5 teaspoons salt
5 ml water
Clean and finely chop the cilantro.

Heat the ghee or oil in a heavy bottomed pan. Toss in the mustard seeds.
Once they have stopped sputtering, add the sesame seeds and fry on a low
flame until they are toasted and fragrant. Be careful not to burn them.
Add the powered spices, closely followed by the chickpea flour. Fry,
stirring, for a minute, then add the yogurt and the water. Stir to get a smooth
batter. Season with salt, and keep cooking over a low flame for 10-15
minutes, stirring often, especially toward the end. It is done if the dough
solidifies when dropped from a teaspoon onto a cold plate. Pour the dough
into an oiled tray and let it cool completely.
Cut it into small diamond shapes and fry both sides of the resulting vadas
in an inch of ghee or oil until golden brown.
Suitable for all three doshas.

Sabudhana Vada
Prearation: 60 minutes
Ingredients:
3 medium potatoes
150 g small pearl tapioca
2 teaspoons cumin
2 tablespoons peanuts
1 green chilli pepper
1 tablespoon grated fresh ginger root
1 tablespoon lemon juice
2 teaspoons salt
a handful of coriander leaves, minced
Soak the tapioca pearls for an hour, then strain them well and squeeze the
water out.
Boil the potatoes till fork tender. Peel them and let them cool down. Once

they are completely cold, shred them coarsely.
Mix all the ingredients and knead them into a cohesive mix. Form small
balls, then flatten them slightly. Fry both sides of the vadas in an inch of
ghee or oil till golden brown. Serve with chutney.
Decreases vata dosha. People with kapha constitution consume in moderation. Not
recommended for people with pitta constitution.

Potato Vada
Preparation: 60 minutes
Ingredients:
5 medium potatoes
a pinch of chilli powder
1 tablespoon fresh grated ginger
1 1/2 teaspoons cumin
½ teaspoon turmeric
¼ teaspoon asafoetida
½ teaspoon ajwain
1 teaspoon sesame seeds
1 1/2 teaspoons salt
a handful of coriander leaves, minced
For the batter:
150 g chickpea flour
½ teaspoon turmeric
½ teaspoon ajwain
a pinch of baking powder
Boil the potatoes until they are soft. Peel and mash them while they are still
hot. Set the smashed potatoes aside to cool completely.
Meanwhile, mix the turmeric, the ajwain, the salt, and the baking powder
into the chickpea flour and add enough water to achieve a thick pancake
batter consistency. Set it aside.
Once the potatoes are cold, add the spices, combine well and form walnut
sized balls out of the mixture. Dip them into the chickpea batter and deep fry
until golden brown.
Decreases vata dosha. People with kapha constitution consume in moderation. Not
recommended for people with pitta constitution.

Samosas
Preparation: 80 minutes
Ingredients:
For the dough:
200 g all purpose flour
200 g whole meal flour
50 g butter
1 1/2 teaspoons salt
about 20 ml water
For the filling:
3 tablespoons ghee or oil
1 ½ teaspoon cumin

2 teaspoons coriander powder
½ teaspoon turmeric
3 medium potatoes, diced
300 g mixed vegetables (to suit one’s dosha)
1 1/2 teaspoons salt
a handful of coriander leaves, minced
1 1/2 teaspoons chat masala
Prepare the dough first. Mix the two kinds of flour, add salt, then rub the
cold butter into the flour. Add enough water to get a soft and pliable, but not
sticky dough. Knead for five minutes, then cover with a damp kitchen towel
and let it rest.
Next, prepare the filling. Heat 3 tablespoons of ghee or oil in a wok or a
large, heavy bottomed frying pan. Add the cumin seeds. Once they are
toasted and fragrant, add the coriander and the turmeric, closely followed by
the vegetables. Season with salt, stir it well, then cover with a tight fitting
lid. Cook the vegetables over medium low flame in their own steam, stirring
occasionally. Once they are soft, add the chaat masala and the coriander
leaves and then coarsely mash the vegetables.
Cool the filling to lukewarm, then start assembling the samosas. Form small
lime sized balls of the dough. Oil your rolling pin and your work surface and
roll the balls into 4 inch diameter disks. Place a heaping tablespoon of filling
on one side of the disk, making sure not to cover the edges. Lightly brush the
edges of the circle with water, then fold the other side of the dough over the
filling and pinch the edges of the dough together. It is important to create a
good seal. To create a decorative seal, hold the samosa in your left hand and,
starting on the left side, pinch the dough flat with the thumb and first finger
of your right hand. Fold it over, and pinch the dough next to the little pleat
you just created. Keep going in this manner until the length of the seal is
pleated. You may want to try to find an online video tutorial for this, or if
you are not feeling adventurous, just use the tins of a fork to decorate your
seal – your samosa will be just as tasty.
Once all the samosas are formed, heat ghee or oil in a deep-frying vessel
and fry the samosas, few at a time, over medium heat. Turn them often. Once
they are golden brown on all sides, drain them and serve them hot with
chutney.

Suitable for people with vata constitution. People with kapha and pitta constitution
should consume in moderation.

Vegetable Pakora
Preparation: 40 minutes
Ingredients:
200 g chickpea flour
1 teaspoon ajwain
2 teaspoons coriander powder
2 teaspoons cumin powder
1 teaspoon turmeric
2-3 teaspoons salt
200-250 ml cold water
700 g vegetable of choice
ghee or oil for deep-frying
Combine the chickpea flour and the spices. Add enough water to get a
smooth, thick batter that coats the back of a spoon. Let it rest for 10-15

minutes.
Meanwhile, clean and chop the vegetables to bite size pieces. Heat ghee or
oil in a deep-frying vessel over medium heat.
Stir the batter again. Adjust the consistency if necessary. Dip the vegetables
into the batter one by one, and immediately drop them into the hot ghee or
oil. Keep the ghee or oil a medium temperature – too hot, and the vegetables
won’t cook through, too cold, and they will soak up the fat. Fry the pakoras
to a nice golden brown color. Drain and serve hot, accompanied by chutney.
Vegetables for the specific doshas:
kapha: zucchini, peppers of all sorts, cauliflower, broccoli, carrots,
beets, eggplant;
pitta: zucchini, cauliflower, broccoli, peppers, potatoes in moderation,
paneer;
vata: potatoes, carrots, beets, winter squash, zucchini, eggplants,
paneer.
Suitable for peopple with vata constitution. People with kapha and pitta constitution
should consume in moderation.

Paneer Tikka
Preparation: 40 minutes
Ingredients:
300 g paneer
5-6 tablespoons yogurt
a pinch of chilli powder
a pinch of turmeric
½ teaspoon chat masala
a pinch of asafoetida
a pinch of ground black peppers
1 teaspoon ajwain
1 teaspoon salt
1 bell pepper
Chop the paneer and the bell pepper into small cubes.
Mix the salt and the spices into the yogurt, then fold in the paneer cubes.
Let them marinate for an hour.

Alternate the paneer cubes and the peppers on a wooden skewer. Heat the
oven to 240 C (450 F). Oil a baking sheet, place the skewers on it, and bake the
paneer and the peppers for 15-20 minutes, until golden brown. Turn them
once midway through baking.
Suitable for all three doshas.

Chutneys and Salads
According to Ayurveda, salads should be prepared ten minutes before serving, in
order to keep the fire of digestion burning. Steaming the vegetables that are used to
make the salad renders them easier to digest. Ayurveda recommends moderation
when it comes to the consumption of salads.

Carrot Chutney
Preparation: 35 minutes
Ingredients:
2 large carrots
2 tablespoons ghee or oil
1 teaspoon black mustard seeds
1 teaspoon cumin
2 teaspoons sesame seeds
3-4 small red chilli peppers (to taste)
4-5 curry leaves
½ teaspoon asafoetida
1 1/2 teaspoons coriander powder
1 teaspoon salt
3 tablespoons cane sugar
½ tablespoon tamarind paste

Clean and slice the carrots. Steam them, then blend them into a smooth
paste.
Heat the ghee or oil in a small frying pan. Add then mustard seeds. When
they finish sputtering, add the cumin seeds. Once the cumin seeds are
toasted and fragrant, add the sesame seeds, the chili peppers and the curry
leaves. Fry for thirty seconds, then sprinkle the asafetida and the coriander
powder. Mix well and add the carrot paste. Season with salt and sugar, and
cook, stirring, until thickened., Take it off the fame and stir in the tamarind
paste.
Helps vata types. People with kapha constitution should consume with moderation.
Increases pitta dosha.

Mango Chutney
Preparation: 30 minutes
Ingredients:
2 tablespoons ghee or oil
1 teaspoon black mustard seeds
4-5 small red chilli peppers (to taste)
½ teaspoon asafoetida
½ teaspoon turmeric
300 g peeled, chopped mangoes
A pinch of salt
3 tablespoons cane sugar
Heat the ghee or oil in a heavy bottomed pan. Add the mustard seeds and
wait until they are done sputtering. Crumble the chili peppers into the oil,
then, after a few seconds, sprinkle in the asafetida and the turmeric powder,
closely followed by the chopped mangoes. Stir well, season with salt and
sugar and cook until the fruit softens and the chutney thickens.
Decreases vata. People with kapha constitution should consume in moderation. Not
recommended for pitta types.

Spinach Chutney
Preparation: 20 minutes
Ingredients:
300 g spinach
2 tablespoons ghee or oil
1 teaspoon black mustard seeds
1 teaspoon urad dal
1 tablespoon shredded coconut
3-4 small red chilli peppers (to taste)
3 curry leaves
¼ teaspoon asafoetida
1 teaspoon cumin powder
¼ teaspoon ground black peppers
2 tablespoons yogurt
1 teaspoon salt
a handful of cilantro

Wash the spinach leaves really well. Chop them finely.
Heat the ghee or oil in a heavy bottomed pan. Add the mustard seeds and
wait till they are done sputtering. Add the urad dal, shredded coconut, chili
powder and curry leaves. Stir over low fire until the beans turn golden brown
and aromatic. Add the asafetida and the cumin powder, stir well, then add
the chopped spinach. Cook, stirring every minute or so, until the spinach
collapses and the water cooks away. Season with salt and pepper, then stir in
the yogurt and the coriander leaves. Heat for a minute, then remove from
the fire.
Suitable for people with kapha constitution. Also suitable for vata types, but they
should use a little more ghee. People with pitta constitution may consume it in
moderation.

Coriander Chutney
Preparation: 15 minutes
Ingredients:
100 g cilantro
2 tablespoons ghee or oil
1 teaspoon black mustard seeds
4 curry leaves
2 green chilli peppers, minced (to taste)
½ teaspoon turmeric
2 tablespoons shredded fresh coconut
Wash and finely mince the coriander leaves.
Heat the ghee or oil in a small, heavy bottomed pan. Add the mustard
seeds. Once they have stopped sputtering, add the curry leaves, the grated
coconut and the minced chili peppers, and stir-fry for another thirty
seconds. Remove from the fire. Sprinkle the spice mixture with turmeric.
Add the coriander leaves and the fried spices to a small blender and blend
them into a thick paste with 50 ml water.
Beneficial for all three doshas.

Cucumber Raita
Preparation: 15 minutes
Ingredients:
2 hothouse cucumbers
300 ml yogurt
1 ½ teaspoons salt
1 teaspoon cumin powder
a pinch of chilli powder
¼ teaspoon asafoetida
Peel and coarsely grate the cucumber. Mix the salt into the grated cucumber

and let it stand for half an hour.
Squeeze as much liquid out of the cucumber as you can. Blend the spices
into the yogurt, then fold in the squeezed out cucumbers. Let it stand for at
least ten minutes to allow the flavors to mingle.
Benefits pepople with pitta constitution. Not recommended with vata and kapha
types.

Winter Squash Salad
Preparation: 20 minutes
Ingredients:
600 g winter squash (weighed after peeling)
2 tablespoons ghee
1 teaspoon black mustard seeds
2 teaspoons urad dal
5-6 curry leaves
a pinch of chilli powder
¼ teaspoon asafoetida
salt
Peel and dice the squash. Steam the diced squash until just tender
Heat ghee or oil in a heavy bottomed pan. Add the black mustard seeds.
Once they have stopped sputtering, add the dal and the curry leaves. Fry
over low heat until the beans turn golden brown and smell aromatic.
Sprinkle in the chili powder and the asafetida, stir, and take off the flame.
Fold the spices into the cooled squash, season with salt and serve.
Decreases kapha and vata. People with pitta constitution should consume in
moderation.

Steamed Salad of Mixed Vegetables
Preparation: 40 minutes
Ingredients:
500 g green beans, trimmed and snapped
300 g carrots, peeled and julienned
half a green chilli pepper
2 teaspoons salt
100 ml yogurt
Steam the green beans. Set it aside. Steam the carrots. Let both vegetables
cool down.
Add the minced green chili pepper, season with salt and fold in the yogurt.
Decreases vata and pitta. People with kapha constitution should use less yogurt.

Sweets
India excels in sweet dishes – and has a passionate love for them. Preparing exotic
deserts is a form of art, kept alive by cooks in ancient temples and generations of
sweetshop owners. Gifting sweets has always been a sign of affection – an easy way to
make someone happy. In hot seasons one offers sweetmeats to guests, since the sweet
taste has a subtle cooling energy.

Carrot Khir
Preparation: 60 minutes
Ingredients:
1 medium carrot, shredded
½ tablespoon ghee
2 cloves
3 cardamom pods
2-3 tablespoons slivered almonds
1 ½ liter full fat milk
6 tablespoons cane sugar
Warm the ghee in a large, heavy bottomed pot. Stir in the cloves and the
cardamom pods, and warm them until they release their enticing aroma. Add
the almonds and the grated carrots, and toast them for 5 minutes. Pour in
the milk and sweeten with sugar. Stir until the sugar dissolves, then keep it
at a gentle roll until it cooks down to about two thirds.
recipe_name: and let it stand for half an hour.

text:
Date Kheer
Preparation: 60 minutes
Ingredients:
½ tablespoon ghee
20 pitted dates
a pinch of ground nutmeg
a pinch of ground cardamom
3 tablespoons cane sugar
8 strands of saffron
1 ½ liter milk
Warm the ghee in a large, heavy bottomed pot. Add the chopped dates, and
stir over medium low flame for two minutes. Sprinkle the nutmeg and
cardamom on the fruit and pour in the milk and the sugar.
Dissolve the saffron in a tablespoon of warmed milk by rubbing the strands
with the back of a small spoon, and then add that to the date mixture, too.
Heat, stirring, until the sugar dissolves, then lower the flame and bring it to

a gentle roll. Cook, stirring often, until it cooks down to two thirds of the
original volume.
Decreases vata and pitta. The spices help kapha type to digest this dish, but they
should only partake in moderation.

Srikhand
Preparation: a few minutes the night before, plus 10 minutes
Ingredients:
800 ml yogurt
4 tablespoons slivered almonds and pistachios, mixed
1 tablespoon rose water
5-6 strands saffron
a pinch of ground cardamom
4-5 tablespoons cane sugar
Place a strainer over a bowl, making sure there is enough space underneath
to contain the liquid that will drip from the yogurt. Place a double layer of
cheesecloth in the strainer. Pour the yogurt into the lined strainer. Cover,
place it into the refrigerator, and let it drip overnight. You should get a
thick, creamy consistency yogurt cheese.
Dissolve the saffron in a tablespoon of warm water by rubbing the strands
with the back of a small spoon. Add it to the yogurt cheese, along with all the

other ingredients. Mix well and serve chilled.
Decreases vata. Suitable for pitta types. Increases kapha.

Gajar ka Halva
Preparation: 35 minutes
Ingredients:
800 g shredded carrots
500 ml milk
100 g cane sugar
½ teaspoon ground cardamom
60 g butter
4 tablespoons slivered almonds
3 tablespoons raisins
½ teaspoon ground cinnamon
Mix the shredded carrots into the milk, pour it into a large, heavy bottomed
pot, and cook for 20-25 minutes, until almost all the milk evaporates. Add the
sugar, the cardamom, the almonds, the butter, the raisins and the cinnamon.
Mix well, and cook, stirring, until the mixture thickens and separates from
the bottom of the pot.

Decreases vata. Not recommended for people with pitta constitution. Kapha types
may consume in moderation.

Besan Laddu
Preparation: 40 minutes
Ingredients:
250 g chickpea flour
150 g butter
4 tablespoons sliced almonds
¼ teaspoon ground cardamom
100 g cane sugar
Melt the butter in a heavy bottomed, wide pan. Add the chickpea flour and
stir over low flame until the flour turns golden brown and gives off a
pleasant, toasted aroma, or about 8-10 minutes.
Transfer the mixture to a bowl, cool to lukewarm, then add the sugar,
almonds and cardamom. Form large balls to make laddus.

Beverages
Beverages are used primarily as medicine. They either perform a specific function
(diuretic, calming, cough suppressant), or are consumed to calm a certain dosha.

Lassi
Preparation: 5 minutes
Ingredients:
200 ml yogurt
150 ml water
1 teaspoon cane sugar
flavoring: rose water for pitta types, cardamom or cinnamon for vata

Preparation is very simple: whisk the ingredients together to make a silky
textured, aromatic yogurt drink.
Decreases vata. People with pitta constitution shoud consume in moderation.
Increases kapha dosha.

Salty Lassi
Preparation: 10 minutes
Ingredients:
200 ml yogurt
150 ml water
½ teaspoon ghee
½ teaspoon black mustard seeds
a pinch of asafoetida
a pinch of cumin powder
a pinch of salt
a pinch of ground ginger
mint leaves for garnish
Heat the ghee in a small frying pan. Toss in the black mustard seeds. Once
they finish sputtering, remove from the fire and stir in the asafetida powder.
Let it cool down. Mix all the ingredients, and whisk them smooth.
A classic vata drink. Calms vata, but increases pitta and kapha.

Ginger Tea
Preparation: 10 minutes
Primarily drunk during winter as medicine against colds and the flu. Ginger
has anti-bacterial and anti-viral propensities. It is an excellent cure for
digestive issues and upper respiratory ailments.
Ingredients:
300 ml water
½-1 tablespoon fresh ginger
1-2 teaspoons honey or cane sugar
Boil the water with the ginger. Simmer 1-5 minutes. The longer you simmer
the tea, the spicier it will get.
Decreases kapha and vata. Increases pitta. If pitta types need ginger as medicine
during the cold months, they should drink ginger water instead of hot ginger tea.
recipe_name: Decreases vata. Not recommended for people with pitta constitution. Kapha types

text:
„Sweet Dreams” Milk
Preparation: 15 minutes
Ingredients:
250 ml milk
2 pitted dates
3 almonds
1 teaspoon shredded coconut
3 strands of saffron
1 teaspoon ghee
a pinch of ground cardamom
1-2 teaspoons honey for vata types, 1 teaspoon cane sugar for pitta
types
Mix everything but the honey. Bring to a simmer, and simmer for 3-4
minutes. Transfer the beverage into a blender, and blend it till smooth. Stir
in the sweetener.
Calms vata and pitta doshas. Increases kapha. It is worth noting, however, that while
vata and pitta types may suffer from insomnia, sleep is almost never a problem for
people with kapha constitution.

Tea for Calming Kapha
People with kapha constitution should avoid sweet herbs. Fruit teas are not
beneficial for them. Bitter herbs are recommended.
Recommended herbal tea mixture:
2 parts basil
3 parts parsley
1 part ground ginger
3 parts yarrow
5 parts stinging nettle
Boil 1 cup of water. Pour it over 1 teaspoon of the herbal mixture. Steep for 5
minutes. Strain.

Tea for Calming Pitta
People with pitta constitution should avoid heating, spicy herbs that inflame
the fire. All herbs in the mint family are beneficial for them, and it is a good
idea to keep those at hand.
Recommended herbal tea mixture:
4 parts blackberry leaves
6 parts lemon balm
1 part fennel
4 parts stinging nettle
2 parts chamomile
Boil 1 cup of water. Pour it over 1 teaspoon of the herbal mixture. Steep for 5
minutes. Strain.
Do not use lemon juice for flavoring. You may use lime juice instead.
Sweeten with cane sugar or fructose, but not honey.

Vata Pacifying Tea
People with vata constitution should avoid bitter and astringent herbs, as
well as herbs with cooling energetics. They should drink herbal teas made
with sweet and pungent herbs.
Recommended tea spice mixture:
1 part ground cinnamon
1 part ground cloves
1 part ground cardamom
1 part ground fennel
1 part ground nutmeg
Simmer 300 ml water with a half a teaspoonful of the spice mixture for a
minute or two. Strain. Sweeten with a teaspoonful of honey.

Nimbu pani
Preparation: 5 minutes
The Indian version of lemonade. A wonderfully cooling drink in the heat of
summer.
Ingredients:
the juice of 2 limes
4-5 tablespoons cane sugar
a pinch of kala namak (black salt)
a pinch of cumin powder
1 ½ l víz
Mix all the ingredients.
Pacifies all three doshas.

Making Paneer (fresh cheese)
The cultured cheese of the West is practically unknown in India. Paneer is a
fresh, homemade, versatile cheese. It can be used in vegetable dishes,
savories, or even sweets.
Ingredients:
2 liters full fat milk
about 6 tablespoons lemon juice
Boil the milk. Meanwhile, set a colander into a bowl, and line it with a double
layer of cheesecloth.
When the milk boils, lower the flame and start adding the lemon juice,
tablespoon by tablespoon. Stir gently, and keep adding lemon juice until the
curds separate and the whey is slightly greenish. Be patient - stir very gently,
and add the lemon juice slowly. If you add too much, the paneer may become
too sour, as well as dry and granular.
Once the curds have separated from the whey, take it off the flame. Let is
set for 10 minutes, then pour it into the strainer.
Fold the cheesecloth over the curds. Place a small flat plate on top, and
weigh it with something heavy – such as a can of tomatoes. Let it drain for an
hour or two. It can be used immediately, but it will stay fresh in the
refrigerator for a couple of days.

Homemade Yogurt
Yogurt is widely used in Indian cuisine. Its mild flavor complements the
richly spiced dishes well.
Ingredients:
2 liters milk
4 tablespoons yogurt
Scald the milk, then let it cool down to 45 °C (113 F). Whip the yogurt into the
warm milk. Cover the pot, wrap it into warm blankets and let it ferment for
5-6 hours. Transfer it to the refrigerator to fully set.

Making Ghee (Purified Butter)
Sometimes ghee is called liquid gold - not an exagaration, for ghee is the
essence of butter, the best of all fats. Ghee has a high smoke point, and its
slightly sweet, nutty flavor lends an irresistible allure to foods cooked in it. It
can be stored at room temperature in a covered container for months.
Ayurveda considers ghee a miracle food:
It is rejuvanating, and slows the process of aging.
It aids digestion, improves memory, and protects the body from
diseases.
It is the best means of detoxing the body.
Nourishes the central nervous system. Pregnant women eat it for the
healthy brain development of the embrio.
Regenerates the body and the mind, enhances the benefits of other
methods of treatment.
Rich in anti-oxidants.
Ingredients:
1–5 kilograms butter
Boil the butter in a large, heavy bottomed pot. Turn the flame as low as
possible, and keep warming the butter without a lid. Take care not to burn it!
If cooked for too long, it will brown and develop an unpleasant aroma. Keep
skimming the foam from the top. When the ghee is done, it turns golden
yellow, transparent, and stops producing foam. Carefully ladle the ghee into
a storage container and let it cool to room temperature.

A few tips for the perfect rice:
Use about 60 g good quality rice (basmati) per person.
Wash the rice, changing the water several times, until the water is no
longer cloudy.
Toast the grains of rice in a small quantity of ghee, butter or oil before
adding the water. Rice cooked thus will be fluffy and non-sticky.
The water for cooking the rice should be 1 ½ times the volume of rice.
Stir the rice a few times after adding the hot water. This helps the
grains to separate.
Most rice recipes rely on steam to cook the grains, so make sure that
you have a tight fitting lid for the rice pot.
Always cook rice on a low flame, without stirring. Stirring rice while
it’s in the pot causes starch to activate and prevents the formation of
steam pockets. This results in uneven cooking and mushy rice.

Glossary
Ajwain (carum ajowan): A celery-sized spice seed, closely related to
caraway and cumin. The assertive flavor resembles thyme, with overtones of
pepper and oregano. Popular in North Indian savories. Aids digestion and
relieves abdominal pain.
Amchoor: A tan colored powder made from sun-dried, tart, unripe mango
slices. It brings pungency to dishes. Amchoor is a primary ingredient in the
spice mix known as chat masala.
Asafoetida (hing): Obtained from several species of ferula, asafoetida is a
dried gum resin. Its characteristic strong odor is due to the sulphur
compounds in the raw substance.
Basmati rice: Light, long grained rice from India and Pakistan. Its superior
aroma and flavor sets it apart from other types of rice.
Curry leaves: The dark green, powerfully aromatic leaves of the plant
murraya koenigii.
Chana dal: A split and husked relative of chickpeas (cicer grietinum).
Popular in Indian cuisine. It is exceptionally delicious, nutritious and easily
digested.
Chaat masala: Indian cuisine’s traditional condiment for freshly sliced fruit.
A sand-colored powdered spice blend predominantly flavored with mango
powder, black salt, and asafoetida.
Chickpeas: A very popular legume in India, and well known in many parts of
the world. An important source of protein, and contains large quantities of
iron and vitamin C. Also known as garbanzo beans, this large, round, tan
bean must be soaked 8 hours or overnight before cooking.
Chickpea flour (besan): A finely milled, almost pale yellow flour made from
roased chana dal. Extensively used for savories and sweets.

Dal: In India, dried legumes are called dal. Also, any soup cooked with
legumes is called dal.
Black salt (kala namak): pinkish gray salt from India. It has a sulfury, eggy
taste.
Black mustard seeds: The tiny round seeds of the the annual Indian
mustard plant brassica juncea. When the mustard seeds are added to hot
ghee or oil, they crackle and turn gray, developing a nutty taste in the
process. It is a pungent and hot spice.
Mung dal: Split mung beans, whether husked or unhusked, are a popular
ingredient in Indian cousine. Easily digested, high in protein and doesn’t take
long to cook.
Garam masala: An aromatic blend of several dry-roasted and ground
„warm” spices. Ayurveda suggests that „warm” spices generate body heat.
Garam masala routinly combines such spices as dry chili peppers, black
peppers, cardamom, coriander, cinnamon, cloves and cumin, but it may
differ from region to region and from household to household. Generally
added to dishes at the end of cooking.
Ghee: Purified butter. It has a sweet, nutty flavor, and a high smokepoint.
Ginger root: The rhizome of the tropical plant zingiber officinale. Native to
and much loved by most of Asia. Relished for its invigorating sharp taste and
medicinal properties. Use grated or julienned. Cannot be substituted with
dry ginger.
Paneer: A simple, non-fermented homemade cheese.
Kalonji: Also known as nigella or black onion seeds, though this small black
seed has no connection to the onion plant. The teardrop shaped seeds have a
peppery taste and, when heated, an aroma reminiscent of oregano. It is an
important ingredient in the five spice blend know as panch puran.
Cardamom: A spice seed harvested from the tropical plant elettaria

cardamomum, a ginger relative native to South India. Cardamom is the third
most expensive spice in the world. Its flavor may be likened to a cross
between lemon zest and eucalyptus. It is a very important ingredient in
sweets.
Coriander seeds: The spherical dried seed of the plant coriandrum sativum.
Tan or brownish in color, warm, and pleasant. Its flavor is mild and sweet,
reminiscent of sage and the fragrance of lemons. Extensively used in savory
dishes.
Coriander leaves: Also known as cilantro. The fresh leaves of the coriander
plant are one of the most universally used fresh herbs on the planet. The fan
shaped leaves are strongly aromatic. The unique warm-bodied flavor of fresh
coriander lends itself well to the highly seasoned cuisine of India, where it is
widely used from dals to savories to chutneys.
Turmeric: The rhizome of the tropical plant curcuma longa. Gives a brilliant
yellow color to dishes. Its flavor is bitter, slightly sour. Turmeric is an
essential ingredient in Indian cuisine, but too much of it will ruin a dish; the
color will be excessive and the flavor bitter.
Fenugreek: Actually a small legume, fenugreek seed comes from the annual
plant trigonella foenumgracum. Used as a spice seed. Its flavor is warm,
bitter. To develop its best flavor, it must be dry-roasted or fried, but only
until lightly toasted. It should not be allowed to turn to reddish-brown
shades because at this point the taste becomes intensely bitter. The fresh or
dried leaves are also much loved in Indian cuisine.
Masala: The term refers to any spice, herb, and seasoning mix. Masalas may
contain as few as two, and as many as 24 ingredients.
Okra: Ladies’ finger. A flowering plant in the mallow family. It is valued for
its edible green pods.
Panch puran: A mix of five whole spices (cumin seeds, black mustard seeds,
fennel seeds, kalonji and fenugreek seeds in equal amounts), most often
associated with Bengali cuisine but also popular in neighboring Orissa and

Bangladesh.
Papadum: Sundried, parchment-thin brittle disks, usually made from spiced
or un-spiced, wet-ground moong or urad dal paste. More often than not, the
disks are deep-fried or open-flame roasted until they swell into delicate
wafers.
Rasam masala: A spice mix from South India. Its ingredients vary from
household to household, but usually include black mustard seeds, coriander,
dry chilli peppers, black peppers, fenugreek, cumin).
Cumin: The seed of the plant cuminum cyminum. Warm, strongly flavored,
mildly bitter.
Rose water: A fragrant water made by steeping rose petals in water. It is
used to flavor sweets and beverages.
Saffron: The most expensive spice in the world. The vivid crimson stigmas
and styles, called threads, are hand-collected and dried. It takes
approximately 70,000 flowers and about 20 man-hours to yield a pound of
saffron. Saffron’s aroma is often described as reminiscent of metallic honey
with grassy or hay-like notes. Its taste is sweet, strong, honey-like. It is also
used as a food coloring agent.
Sambar masala: A powdered spice mix from South India. Many versions
exist, but most use chilli powder, dry curry leaves, roasted coriander seeds,
cumin, black mustard, fenugreek, black peppers, turmeric, sesame seeds,
chana dal, toor dal and urad dal.
Tamarind: The acidulous pulp of the pod-like fruit of the tamarind tree.
Urad dal: Also called black lentils. Urad dal has been in cultivation in India
from ancient times. It is widely used in the Punjabi cuisine and as an
ingredient of savory snacks.
